{{smaller|''ness'', etc.) may be regarded as formed from the adjective in ''un-'', with the adverbial or noun formative (< ''unfair'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>, ''unfair'' + ''-ness''), or as formed from such derived forms by prefixing the negative (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fairly'', ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fairness'', etc.). (''b'') It is prefixed to some nouns to express the absence, incompleteness, or the contrary of what the noun expresses, as in ''unrest'', ''untruth'', ''unwisdom'', ''undress''. Before an adjective in ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>, ''un-'' is nearly equivalent to ''-less'' after a noun: ''unresting'' is nearly equivalent to ''restless'', ''unchanging'' to ''changeless'', etc. This negative may be prefixed to any adjective or participle whatever, whether of native or of foreign origin. It is equivalent to its cognate ''in-''<sup>3</sup> of Latin origin, ''an-''<sup>5</sup>, ''a-''<sup>18</sup> of Greek origin, and also to ''non-'', sometimes to ''dis-'', etc., of Latin origin (the Latin forms, ''in-''<sup>3</sup>, etc., being used chiefly before adjectives of Latin origin, but also before other adjectives): thus, ''uncomplete'', ''incomplete'', and potentially ''noncomplete''; ''unelastic'', ''inelastic'', ''non-elastic''; ''unemphatic'', ''nonemphatic'', etc.; ''unreputable'', ''disreputable'', etc. As ''un-''<sup>1</sup> may be prefixed to any adjective or participle whatever, it is needless, and it would be impracticable, to include all such formations in the dictionary. In the following pages only such are entered and defined as have had a special development, are used in senses not merely reversing the original adjective, or are in Middle English or Anglo-Saxon use, and so form the basis of all the later compounds, or are for other reasons noteworthy. For the meaning and history of the other forms in ''un-''<sup>1</sup>, see the corresponding simple forms. Of the forms here entered the etymology is usually obvious, and it is therefore not expressly given, except in the older and the exceptional words; the history will be found under the simple form. See also ''un-''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''un-'''<sup>2</sup>. [< ME. ''un-'', ''on-'', < AS. ''un-'', ''on-'', ''ond-'', ''an-'', ''and-'' (as in ''on-lūcan'', unlock, ''on-leósan'', unloose, etc.), a particular use of ''an-'', ''and-'', back, against, = G. ''ent-'', etc.: see ''and-'', ''an-''<sup>2</sup>, ''a-''<sup>5</sup>. This prefix has been more or less confused with ''un-''<sup>1</sup>, the notion of reversal in the one (AS. ''un-'', ''on-'', etc., ‘back’) being in many cases practically identical with the notion of negation in the other
readings.c1s3: (AS. ''un-'', ‘not’). There are three different senses possible to a form with the prefix in ''un-''<sup>2</sup> and the suffix ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>—e. g., ''unarmed'' may mean (''a'') ‘not now armed’ (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''armed'', ''p. a.''); (''b'') ‘not yet armed’ (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''armed'', pp.); (''c'') ‘that has been deprived of arms,’ ‘no longer armed’ (pp. of ''unarm'', i. e. < ''unarm'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>). So ''unlocked'', (''a'') ‘not now locked’ (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''locked'', ''p. a.''); (''b'') ‘not yet locked’ (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''locked'', pp.); (''c'') ‘no longer locked,’ ‘open’ (pp. of ''unlock'', i. e. < ''unlock'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>); ''unlearned'', (''a'') ‘not learned,’ ‘ignorant’ (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''learned'', ''a.''); (''b'') ‘not yet learned’ (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''learned'', pp.); (''c'') ‘no longer learned,’ ‘rejected’ (pp. of ''unlearn'', i. e. < ''unlearn'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>); etc.] An inseparable prefix of verbs (generally transitive), meaning ‘back,’ and denoting the reversal or annulment of the action of the simple verb: as, ''undo'', ''unlearn'', ''unlock'', ''unmake'', etc. {{smaller|It is very common as prefixed to verbs made from nouns, implying privation of the object named by the noun, or the qualities connoted by it: as, ''unarm'', ''uncowl'', ''unfrock'', ''unhelm'', ''unhorse'', etc., to take off or deprive of one’s arms, cowl, frock, helm, horse, etc.; ''unman'', ''unsex'', to deprive of the qualities of a man, of sex, etc. When used with verbs denoting utterance (which cannot actually be reversed or undone), it implies retractation: as, to ''unsay'', ''unspeak'', ''unswear'', etc. Words with this prefix are much confused with words having the prefix ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (see etymology). In the following pages words with the prefix ''un-''<sup>2</sup> are generally so marked, while words with the prefix ''un-''<sup>1</sup> are left without etymological note, except in special cases. See remarks under ''un-''<sup>1</sup>.}}

And seten so til euensonge and songen ''vmwhile''.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 345.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Throgh whiche treason betydes, & ternys ''emquehile''
Bolde men to batell and biker with hond;
That draghes vnto dethe, & deris full mony.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2943.}}}}
{{smaller block|Miss Barbara Clinkscale, daughter to the ''umquhile'', and sister to the then existing Clinkscale of that ilk.
{{right|''Scott'', Pirate, iv.}}}}

'''umzumbit''' (ûm-zûm′bit), ''n.'' [Native name, said to mean ‘ironwood.’] A leguminous South African tree, ''Milletia Caffra'', or its wood. {{smaller|The tree grows 20 or 30 feet high; its wood is of a brown color, is very hard and close-grained, and is said to surpass lignum-vitæ in resistance to wear, and to be impervious to the teredo; it is used for bearings, walking-sticks, tool-handles, etc.}}

’'''un''', ''n.'' A dialectal corruption of ''one''. {{smaller|It is common in the southern United States, in the phrases ''we ’uns'', ''you ’uns'', a sort of expanded plural, equivalent to ''we all'', ''you all'', which are used in much the same way.}}

''an-'', ''a-''; a common negative prefix, meaning ‘not.’ Cf. ''un-''<sup>2</sup>.] An inseparable prefix, meaning ‘not.’ {{smaller|(''a'') It is prefixed to adjectives (including participles) and to adverbs, to express simply the negative, as ''unable'', ''unfair'', ''untrue'', ''unwise'', etc., ''unbending'', ''unyielding'', ''undoubting'', ''unchanging'', ''unthinking'', etc., ''unbent'', ''undoubted'', ''unchanged'', etc., ‘not able,’ ‘not fair,’ etc. The adverbs or nouns derived from such adjectives or participles (as ''unfairly'', ''unfairness'', etc.) may be regarded as formed from the adjective in ''un-'', with the adverbial or noun formative (< ''unfair'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>, ''unfair'' + ''-ness''), or as formed from such derived forms by prefixing the negative (< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fairly'', ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fairness'', etc.). (''b'') It is prefixed to some nouns to express the absence, incompleteness, or the contrary of what the noun expresses, as in ''unrest'', ''untruth'', ''unwisdom'', ''undress''. Before an adjective in ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>, ''un-'' is nearly equivalent to ''-less'' after a noun: ''unresting'' is nearly equivalent to ''restless'', ''unchanging'' to ''changeless'', etc. This negative may be prefixed to any adjective or participle whatever, whether of native or of foreign origin. It is equivalent to its cognate ''in-''<sup>3</sup> of Latin origin, ''an-''<sup>5</sup>, ''a-''<sup>18</sup> of Greek origin, and also to ''non-'', sometimes to ''dis-'', etc., of Latin origin (the Latin forms, ''in-''<sup>3</sup>, etc., being used chiefly before adjectives of Latin origin, but also before other adjectives): thus, ''uncomplete'', ''incomplete'', and potentially ''noncomplete''; ''unelastic'', ''inelastic'', ''non-elastic''; ''unemphatic'', ''nonemphatic'', etc.; ''unreputable'', ''disreputable'', etc. As ''un-''<sup>1</sup> may be prefixed to any adjective or participle whatever, it is needless, and it would be impracticable, to include all such formations in the dictionary. In the following pages only such are entered and defined as have had a special development, are used in senses not merely reversing the original adjective, or are in Middle English or Anglo-Saxon use, and so form the basis of all the later compounds, or are for other reasons noteworthy. For the meaning and history of the other forms in ''un-''<sup>1</sup>, see the corresponding simple forms. Of the forms here entered the etymology is usually obvious, and it is therefore not expressly given, except in the older and the exceptional words; the history will be found under the simple form. See also ''un-''<sup>2</sup>.}}

''ent-'', etc.: see ''and-'', ''an-''<sup>2</sup>, ''a-''<sup>5</sup>. This prefix has been more or less confused with ''un-''<sup>1</sup>, the notion of reversal in the one (AS.
